title: Project 6: inventory manager with structures and file persistence
learningObjectives: Model products with a structure containing a unique ID, name, quantity and integer-cent unit price.
Manage a variable number of products using a dynamically resized array with separate count and capacity values.
Implement add, list, search, stock-in and stock-out operations while enforcing inventory rules.
Persist an inventory snapshot to a text file and load records with validation when the program starts.
Handle allocation failures, malformed or duplicate file records, insufficient stock and file I/O errors.
Detect low stock and prevent quantity and monetary arithmetic from overflowing their integer types.

understand.concept: An inventory manager stores a changing collection of products. Each product has a unique positive ID, a name, a non-negative stock quantity and a positive unit price. The project represents each product with struct Product and stores products in a dynamically allocated array. The collection tracks count (active products) and capacity (allocated slots). It supports adding products, listing and searching, receiving stock, issuing stock, low-stock warnings, and saving/loading the collection from a text file. Money is stored as integer cents to avoid floating-point rounding in totals and displayed prices.
understand.whyItMatters: Inventory software combines data modeling, dynamic collections, business rules and persistent storage. It is a realistic exercise in keeping in-memory state consistent with validated data read from and written to a file.
understand.analogy: Think of the product array as the live stock register in a shop and the text file as its saved snapshot. Stock-in adds units; stock-out removes units only when enough are available.
understand.analogyLimit: A simple text file is not a database. It does not automatically provide transactions, concurrent-user safety, backups or recovery from every power failure. The program must validate records and report I/O errors.

explain.narrative:
Each struct Product contains an integer ID, a bounded name array, an integer quantity and a long long price_cents value. IDs must be positive and unique. Quantity may be zero but never negative. A price must be positive. The dynamic array grows when required: reserve_products checks the requested element count against SIZE_MAX / sizeof *items, uses realloc through a temporary pointer and updates capacity only after success. This preserves the original allocation if growth fails.

The business operations are separate from terminal input. Searching scans only the active range. Stock-in checks that adding a quantity cannot exceed INT_MAX. Stock-out rejects an amount larger than the available quantity. Low-stock display marks products with five or fewer units; this threshold is an explicit example rule and can be changed.

The file format is one record per line: id|name|quantity|price_cents. The name cannot contain the pipe delimiter. On startup, the program opens inventory.txt in read mode, parses each complete line into a temporary Product, validates all fields, and adds only valid non-duplicate records. Malformed and duplicate records are skipped and counted. An absent file is treated as a new empty inventory.

Saving writes a complete snapshot to inventory.tmp, checks each fprintf and fclose result, then renames the temporary file to inventory.txt. The temporary file is created in the same directory so the rename can act as a replacement step on common hosted systems. C implementations may differ in how rename behaves when the destination already exists; the program reports a replacement failure rather than claiming the save succeeded. This teaching project does not implement fsync, multi-process locking or guaranteed crash durability.

Changes made in memory are not automatically saved. Choose the Save menu option after changes. If the program exits or the machine stops before saving, unsaved changes may be lost. Before using the example with important data, keep a backup of inventory.txt. All file contents are plain text.

examples.title: Test inventory operations and stock rules
examples.explanation: This deterministic program tests dynamic allocation, product validation, duplicate-ID rejection, search, stock-in, insufficient-stock rejection, price update, deletion and cleanup. It isolates the core inventory operations from file and menu input so the business rules can be tested predictably.

examples.title: Complete file-backed inventory manager
examples.explanation: The interactive program loads inventory.txt at startup, supports adding and searching products, lists low-stock items, receives and issues stock, and saves a validated snapshot when requested. It uses integer cents for prices, checks dynamic allocation and file operations, and frees the product array before exit. Save explicitly after changes.

practise.guidedTask: Run the first example and trace how the inventory count and capacity change as products are added. Then trace a stock-in operation and a rejected stock-out operation. Explain why a product quantity cannot become negative.
practise.independentTask: Extend the inventory manager with a validated unit-price update option and a report showing the total stock value. Calculate each product's quantity multiplied by its price_cents with overflow checks, and check the sum before adding it to the report total. Test duplicate IDs, zero and negative prices, zero stock, insufficient stock, quantity overflow, malformed file lines, duplicate records in the file, an absent file, a failed save and a low-stock boundary of five versus six units.
hints: Keep product identity and business rules in struct Product and the inventory operation functions.
Use count for active records and capacity for allocated slots; never iterate to capacity when listing products.
Check allocation-size arithmetic before multiplying a count by sizeof an element.
Store money in integer cents and validate the input format before converting it.
Parse a file line into a temporary product and validate every field before adding it to the live inventory.
A successful in-memory change is not persistent until the save operation completes and reports success.

questions.prompt: Why does the inventory manager keep count and capacity separately?
options: Count tracks active products while capacity tracks allocated array slots.
Count stores the largest product ID and capacity stores the price.
They both represent the number of bytes in the file.
questions.answer: Count tracks active products while capacity tracks allocated array slots.
questions.explanation: Only the first count elements are active; capacity is the storage currently available.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a stock-out request exceeds the available quantity?
options: Reject the operation and leave the quantity unchanged.
Allow the quantity to become negative.
questions.answer: Reject the operation and leave the quantity unchanged.
questions.explanation: The inventory invariant requires every product quantity to remain non-negative.

questions.prompt: Why is price stored as integer cents in this project?
options: To avoid common floating-point rounding issues in currency arithmetic.
Because printf cannot display decimal numbers.
questions.answer: To avoid common floating-point rounding issues in currency arithmetic.
questions.explanation: Integer minor units provide exact addition within the representable range, provided overflow is checked.

questions.prompt: What is the safest approach when loading a product line from the file?
options: Parse into a temporary structure, validate all fields and then add it.
Copy the line directly over an existing product.
Assume every line is correctly formatted.
questions.answer: Parse into a temporary structure, validate all fields and then add it.
questions.explanation: Validation before committing prevents malformed or duplicate file data from corrupting live state.

questions.prompt: When can the program report that a snapshot save succeeded?
options: After all records are written, the stream closes successfully and the replacement step succeeds.
As soon as fopen returns a non-null pointer.
Immediately after the first product is printed.
questions.answer: After all records are written, the stream closes successfully and the replacement step succeeds.
questions.explanation: Buffered writes and the final rename can fail, so the full save sequence must be checked.
